activities.title: Practical Context: Counterfeit Cargo Containers & Label Tampering
activities.description: How mismatched compile-time labels and runtime physical realities create catastrophic runtime failures.
activities.content:
Imagine an automated shipping port. Every shipping container has a physical barcode scanner on the bottom that inspects weight and contents during transit. If you label a container 'Fragile Porcelain' on paper (compile-time type), but the physical crate at runtime has no internal type verification, someone can load heavy scrap metal into it. The moment an automated crane lifts it expecting 50 kilograms, it snaps and destroys the facility.

Java arrays are physical containers: they know their exact type at runtime (`reified`) and enforce it on every write (`ArrayStoreException`). Generics are paper manifests: the compiler validates types, but erases them completely at runtime (`erased`). When developers try to combine erased manifests with reified containers (`new T[10]`), or change the contents of a sealed container after indexing (`mutable HashMap keys`), the system experiences catastrophic runtime crashes (heap pollution, lost keys, and ClassCastExceptions).

activities.title: Top 5 Collections & Generics Interview Pitfalls
activities.description: Exhaustive technical dissection of array reification vs erasure, heap pollution, mutable map keys, subList invalidation, and primitive array boxing.
activities.content:
### Formal Computer Science Definition
A language runtime anomaly occurs when static type verification guarantees are bypassed due to type erasure, covariant array assignments, or mutable state violation of collection indexing invariants, resulting in heap pollution, silent lookup failures, or unexpected runtime exceptions.

### The 5 Classic Gotchas Dissected

```
                         Collections & Generics Gotchas
                                       |
       +-------------------+-----------+-----------+-------------------+
       |                   |                       |                   |
1. Generic Arrays    2. Heap Pollution       3. Mutable Keys     4. subList Trap
- new T[10] banned   - List<String>...       - Mutating key      - Mutating parent
- Reified vs Erased  - @SafeVarargs fix        breaks hash bucket  invalidates view
```

#### 1. Why `new T[10]` is Forbidden
- **Arrays are Reified and Covariant**: An array knows its component type at runtime and checks every element store (`String[]` knows it only holds Strings; `Object[] arr = new String[1]; arr[0] = 123;` throws `ArrayStoreException`). Furthermore, `String[]` is a subtype of `Object[]`.
- **Generics are Erased and Invariant**: Type parameters (`T`) are erased to `Object` (or bound) at compile time. At runtime, the JVM has no idea what `T` is.
- **The Conflict**: If `new T[10]` were allowed, the compiler would create `new Object[10]`. If assigned to `T[]` where `T = String`, code could write integers into it, destroying the type safety guarantee of generics without triggering `ArrayStoreException`.
- **The Solution**: Use `(T[]) Array.newInstance(clazz, capacity)` or pass a generator `IntFunction<T[]>`.

#### 2. Heap Pollution and `@SafeVarargs`
Varargs (`T... args`) is syntactic sugar for array allocation (`new T[] args`). When combined with generics, Java is forced to allocate a raw array: `new List[args.length]`.
- **Heap Pollution**: Occurs when a variable of a parameterized type references an object that is not of that type.
- If a method modifies the array or exposes it to untrusted code, runtime `ClassCastException` results.
- **`@SafeVarargs` Rule**: Use `@SafeVarargs` **only** when:
  1. The method does not store anything into the varargs array.
  2. The method does not allow the reference to the varargs array to escape.

#### 3. The Mutable Key / Set Element Trap
`HashMap` calculates bucket index via `hash(key.hashCode()) & (table.length - 1)` at the moment `put()` is called.
- If an instance field that participates in `hashCode()` or `equals()` is subsequently mutated, the key's hash code changes.
- Future calls to `map.get(key)` calculate the **new** bucket index and search a completely different bucket!
- The original entry remains orphaned in the old bucket: `map.containsKey(key)` returns `false`, yet the entry cannot be garbage-collected, creating a **silent memory leak**.
- **Golden Rule**: Map keys and Set elements must be strictly immutable (e.g., Java `record`, `String`, `UUID`, primitive wrappers).

#### 4. The `subList` Structural Mutation Invalidation
`List.subList(from, to)` returns a view over the backing list with an internal `expectedModCount`.
- If the **backing list** is structurally modified (e.g. `list.add("item")`) after the sublist is created, any subsequent call on `subList` (e.g. `subList.size()`) detects `modCount != expectedModCount` and immediately throws `ConcurrentModificationException`—even in a single-threaded program!
- Any mutations must be performed **through the sublist itself** (`subList.add(...)`).

#### 5. Primitive Array `Arrays.asList(int[])` Trap
Generics require reference types. When passing a primitive array `int[] nums = {1, 2, 3};` to `Arrays.asList(nums)`:
- The compiler cannot bind `T` to `int`.
- Instead, it binds `T` to `int[]` (an array is an Object!).
- The returned list is a `List<int[]>` of **size 1** whose single element is the entire primitive array!

questions.question: Why does calling 'new T[10]' cause a compilation error in Java?
options: Because the JVM does not have sufficient heap memory for generic allocations
Because arrays are reified (they require runtime knowledge of component type), whereas generic types are erased at compile-time
Because generics only support single object references
Because generic arrays must extend Serializable
questions.explanation: Arrays require exact runtime type information to enforce ArrayStoreException. Because generic type parameters are erased at compile-time to Object, the JVM cannot reify the array's true element type, making generic array creation illegal.

questions.question: What is the result of executing Arrays.asList(new int[]{1, 2, 3}).size()?
options: Compilation error because int is not an Object
questions.explanation: Arrays.asList(T... a) expects reference types. Because int is primitive, the entire int[] array matches T as a single Object, resulting in a List<int[]> containing 1 element.

questions.question: What causes a ConcurrentModificationException when calling subList.get(0) in a single-threaded program?
options: The subList index was out of bounds
The parent backing list was structurally modified (e.g., add or remove) after the subList view was created
The garbage collector reclaimed the subList
questions.explanation: subList maintains an expectedModCount matching the backing list. If the parent list is structurally modified directly, modCount changes, and any subsequent interaction with the sublist detects the mismatch and throws ConcurrentModificationException.

questions.question: What is heap pollution in Java, and under what conditions can a developer safely annotate a method with @SafeVarargs?
questions.answer:
Heap pollution occurs when a variable of a parameterized type refers to an object that is not of that parameterized type (e.g., a List<String> reference pointing to a List<Integer> object). This usually arises when generic varargs methods (which compile to raw Object[] arrays) allow unsafe references to escape or overwrite array slots.

A developer can safely annotate a method with @SafeVarargs if and only if:
1. The method does not write or store any elements into the varargs array parameter.
2. The method does not allow the reference to the varargs array to escape (i.e., it is not returned, assigned to an external field, or passed to untrusted code).
If the method merely iterates over the varargs elements to read them, it is safe.

questions.question: How can an object in a HashMap become un-retrievable, and why does this cause a memory leak?
questions.answer:
When an object is used as a HashMap key, its bucket index is computed from key.hashCode(). If an instance field contributing to hashCode() is mutated after insertion, the object's hash code changes.

When map.get(key) or map.remove(key) is subsequently called with that same object, the HashMap calculates the new hash code and searches the corresponding new bucket, finding nothing (null). The entry remains stuck in the original bucket indefinitely. Because the HashMap's table retains a hard reference to the key and value, neither can be garbage-collected, creating a silent memory leak that grows over time.

practiceProblems.title: Type-Safe Generic Array Allocator
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement `<T> T[] createGenericArray(Class<T> clazz, int capacity)` using `java.lang.reflect.Array.newInstance` to dynamically allocate a reified generic array of the specified capacity.

practiceProblems.title: Primitive Array Boxed Converter
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement `List<Integer> convertPrimitiveArray(int[] numbers)` that correctly converts a primitive `int[]` into a `List<Integer>` of matching size, avoiding the `Arrays.asList(int[])` single-element trap.

practiceProblems.title: Safe SubList Extraction and Detachment
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement `List<String> getDetachedSubList(List<String> source, int fromIndex, int toIndex)` that returns a completely detached copy of the sublist slice so that subsequent modifications to `source` do not invalidate the returned list.

practiceProblems.title: Safe Varargs Collector
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a generic method `@SafeVarargs public static <T> List<T> safeCollect(T... items)` that returns an unmodifiable List of items without causing heap pollution. If items is null, return `List.of()`.

practiceProblems.title: Immutable Key Wrapper for HashMap
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement an immutable key wrapper `record SecureKey(String tenantId, String resourceId)` to prevent hash bucket corruption when used as a HashMap key. Implement `String getLookupKey(Map<SecureKey, String> map, String tenantId, String resourceId)`.
